sentences.text: They went back to the cottage.
Bríd made tea.
It was still early afternoon, but the sky had gone grey the way it does in the west of Ireland, and the little kitchen was dim, and Bríd lit the small oil lamp on the table.
She poured two mugs of strong tea and sat down opposite Aisling.
She was quiet for a long moment.
Then she began.

"When a person on the island knew they were going to die," she said, "and this was a hundred years ago, two hundred years ago — they might take a small piece of chalk, or a piece of charred stick from the fire, and they would write something on the underside of a specific stone.
Something they wanted to leave.
Not for their family, especially.
For whoever came after.
For anyone who bothered to look.
Then they would scratch a small mark on the top of that stone, so someone could find it.
Sometimes three little lines.
Sometimes a dot.
Sometimes a spiral.
Every family had their own mark."
Aisling said, "But you said it hadn't been done in fifty years." Bríd said, "No.
It stopped about the time of the war.
People stopped believing in it, or stopped thinking there would be anyone in the future who would care to find one.
The world got smaller.
People started writing letters instead, and putting them in envelopes, and posting them.
It is not the same.
A letter is written to someone.
A stone is left for whoever."
Aisling asked, "What did people write?" Bríd said, "Anything.
My grandmother said it was often not important things.
It was often a piece of advice, or a joke, or a memory, or a name of someone they had loved that nobody else remembered.
Sometimes it was a warning.
My grandmother told me she once found one that said, in the old Irish, do not trust the man with the yellow boat.
She was thirteen when she found it.
The man with the yellow boat had been dead for eighty years by then.
But she never forgot the message.
She told me she always thought of it as advice from a friend."
Aisling laughed.
Bríd smiled, which was rare, and drank her tea.
Bríd was quiet for a moment.
Then she said, "My mother left one." Aisling sat still.
Bríd went on.
"Her name was Peig.
She died in nineteen sixty-six.
I was eighteen.
Before she died, she told me she had done it.
She said, if you ever want to find it, it is on the island.
Somewhere.
She did not tell me where.
She said, you will know when you want to look." Bríd smiled without any lightness in it.
"I did not want to look.
Not for a long time.
I do not really know why.
Maybe because as long as I did not look, it was still waiting for me.
If I found it, then whatever she had said would be a real thing, and I could not un-know it.
Sixty years I have not looked."
Aisling did not know what to say.
She sat and waited.
Bríd said, "But your mother told me you were coming.
And I thought, this girl has never been to Inishmore.
And I thought — maybe now.
Maybe with the child here, it will be time."
They went out that afternoon.
Bríd walked ahead and Aisling followed.
They walked to the west side of the island, toward a spot where three fields Bríd's family had once owned came down to meet the sea.
"My mother built two walls in her life," Bríd said.
"Most people didn't build walls — you inherited them and mended them.
But there was a bad storm when she was young that knocked down two long stretches near her father's fields, and she and her brother rebuilt them.
That was in nineteen twenty-eight.
She would have put her stone in one of those two walls."
Bríd showed her the two walls.
One ran along the top of a low headland, high above the sea.
The other cut down a slope toward a small stony beach.
Both were long — longer than Aisling had thought when Bríd had said "a stretch of wall." Together they held maybe six hundred stones each.
Somewhere in one of them, if it was still there, was Peig's stone.
They walked slowly along the top wall.
Aisling had never looked at stones so closely in her life.
Most of them were plain.
But every now and then she found one that had something — a natural line, a scratch, a spot of lichen that looked like a mark.
She kept calling Bríd over.
Bríd kept looking and shaking her head.
"Natural.
That's just the stone breaking.
That's just weather."
Then Aisling found one that made her heart jump.
Halfway along the wall, at just about the height of her shoulder, was a stone with a small deliberate circle carved on it, and inside the circle, two letters — P.M.
She called Bríd.
Bríd came.
Bríd looked.
She was quiet for a moment.
Then she smiled a small smile that had a lot in it, and shook her head.
"No, love.
That is not hers.
That is Peig Mullen — an old woman who lived on this end of the island a hundred and twenty years ago, no relation.
Different Peig.
My mother would never have put her own initials.
That was not the way.
You did it in secret.
If your name was on it, it was to be found because you wanted it found.
That was different.
My mother wanted her stone found only by someone who was really looking."
Aisling was disappointed.
Bríd saw.
Bríd said, "But that was good work.
You are learning to see."
